topic: Bulk Packaging Placarding Threshold
question: A bulk package is a single container with a capacity greater than how many gallons, and how must it be placarded?
choice_a: Greater than 500 gallons, and placards are only required when the tank is completely full
choice_b: Greater than 55 gallons, and it never needs placards regardless of contents
choice_c: Greater than 1,000 gallons, and only the shipper's name needs to be displayed
choice_d: Greater than 119 gallons, and it must be placarded even if it only contains the residue of a hazardous material
explanation: The manual defines bulk packaging as a single container with a capacity greater than 119 gallons, and states that a bulk package, and the vehicle carrying it, must be placarded even if it only has the residue of a hazardous material.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Bulk Packaging and Placarding

topic: Illegal to Transport Leaking Packages
question: You notice a package of hazardous materials is leaking before you leave the shipper's dock. What must you do?
choice_a: Load it at the back of the trailer away from other freight and proceed
choice_b: Do not transport it, since it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials
choice_c: Tape over the leak and continue the trip as scheduled
choice_d: Continue the trip but drive at a reduced speed
explanation: The manual warns that leaks spell trouble and that it is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials, so a leaking package must not be transported.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Loading and Unloading Precautions

topic: No-Smoking Classes During Loading and Unloading
question: While loading or unloading hazardous materials, you must never allow smoking near which of the following hazard classes?
choice_a: Only Class 9 (Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials)
choice_b: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_c: Only materials that are also marked as marine pollutants
choice_d: Only Class 7 (Radioactive Materials)
explanation: The manual lists Class 1, Class 2.1, Class 3, Class 4, and Class 5 as the hazard classes around which smoking must never be allowed while loading or unloading.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - No Smoking When Loading or Unloading

topic: Cargo Heater Restrictions When Loading
question: The special cargo heater loading rules, which usually forbid the use of cargo heaters (including automatic heater/air conditioner units), apply to which hazard classes?
choice_a: All nine hazard classes equally
choice_b: Class 6 (Poison) and Class 9 (Miscellaneous) only
choice_c: Class 8 (Corrosives) only
choice_d: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids)
explanation: The manual states there are special cargo heater rules for loading Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), which usually forbid cargo heater use.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Cargo Heater Rules

topic: Closed Cargo Space Requirement
question: You cannot have overhang or tailgate loads of Class 1 (Explosives), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), or Class 5 (Oxidizers) unless the packages meet what condition?
choice_a: They weigh less than 50 pounds each
choice_b: They are fire and water resistant, or covered with a fire and water resistant tarp, and are loaded in a closed cargo space
choice_c: They are wrapped in plastic sheeting only
choice_d: They are placed at least 10 feet from the cab
explanation: The manual requires these hazard classes to be loaded into a closed cargo space unless all packages are fire and water resistant or covered with a fire and water resistant tarp.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Use Closed Cargo Space

topic: Class 1 Explosives - Preparing to Load or Unload
question: Before loading or unloading any explosives, what must you do to your cargo heaters and their power/fuel supply?
choice_a: Set the cargo heaters to their lowest setting but leave them running
choice_b: Nothing; cargo heaters do not need to be addressed for explosives
choice_c: Disable the cargo heaters, disconnect the heater power sources, and drain the heater fuel tanks
choice_d: Only disconnect the power source but leave the fuel tank full
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to turn off the engine, then disable cargo heaters, disconnect heater power sources, and drain heater fuel tanks before loading or unloading explosives.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Precautions for Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

topic: Floor Lining for Explosives
question: When a floor lining is required for Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what material must it be?
choice_a: Either non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal, with the floor kept tight
choice_b: Rubber matting over an iron floor
choice_c: Stainless steel plating bolted to the floor
choice_d: Any metal, as long as it is painted
explanation: The manual states the floor must be tight and the liner must be either non-metallic material or non-ferrous metal (metal that does not contain iron or iron alloys).
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Precautions for Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

topic: Emergency Roadside Transfer of Explosives
question: Under what circumstances may you transfer Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives from one vehicle to another on a public roadway?
choice_a: Any time it is convenient to do so
choice_b: Only in an emergency, and you must set out red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns to warn others
choice_c: Only if a law enforcement officer directs traffic during the transfer
choice_d: Only at night, without any warning devices needed
explanation: The manual says you must not transfer these explosives between vehicles on a public roadway except in an emergency, and if an emergency transfer is required, you must set out red warning reflectors, flags, or electric lanterns.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Precautions for Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

topic: Never Transport Damaged or Damp Explosives
question: At the shipper's dock, you notice a package of explosives shows dampness and an oily stain. What should you do?
choice_a: Load it only if it is wrapped in an extra tarp
choice_b: Refuse to transport it, since you should never transport a package of explosives that shows any dampness or oily stain
choice_c: Load it, but place it farthest from the cab
choice_d: Wipe it down and load it as usual
explanation: The manual states that you should never transport damaged packages of explosives and should not take a package that shows any dampness or oily stain.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Precautions for Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

topic: Class 4 and 5 Materials - Moisture and Ventilation
question: Class 4 (Flammable Solids) and Class 5 (Oxidizers) materials that become unstable and dangerous when wet must be handled how during loading, unloading, and transit?
choice_a: Loaded only in the rain to keep dust down
choice_b: Stored in a sealed, airtight compartment with no ventilation
choice_c: Kept dry, and materials subject to spontaneous combustion or heating must be in vehicles with sufficient ventilation
choice_d: Sprayed lightly with water to reduce dust before loading
explanation: The manual requires that materials which become unstable when wet be kept dry during transit, loading, and unloading, and that materials subject to spontaneous combustion or heating be kept in vehicles with sufficient ventilation.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 4 and 5 Materials

topic: Class 8 Corrosives - Loading and Nitric Acid Rule
question: When hand-loading breakable containers of corrosive liquid, and when handling nitric acid, what does the manual require?
choice_a: Load breakable containers one by one, right side up, without dropping or rolling them, and never load nitric acid above any other product
choice_b: Roll the containers gently into place to reduce lifting strain
choice_c: Load nitric acid first at the bottom, then stack any other product directly on top of it
choice_d: Stack breakable containers upside down to protect the caps, and load nitric acid on the very top regardless of other cargo
explanation: The manual instructs loading breakable corrosive containers one by one, right side up, without dropping or rolling them, and specifically states not to load nitric acid above any other product.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 8 (Corrosive) Materials

topic: Corrosive Liquids - Prohibited Nearby Loading
question: According to the manual, corrosive liquids must never be loaded next to or above which of the following?
choice_a: Empty, cleaned packaging of any kind
choice_b: Non-hazardous general freight such as furniture
choice_c: Division 4.1 (Flammable Solids) and Class 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_d: Other Class 8 (Corrosive) materials of the same type
explanation: The manual lists Division 4.1 (Flammable Solids) and Class 5 (Oxidizers), among others, as materials that corrosive liquids must never be loaded next to or above.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 8 (Corrosive) Materials

topic: Charged Storage Batteries - Loading Precautions
question: How must charged storage batteries be loaded, and what may they never be loaded with?
choice_a: Stacked directly on top of one another with no restrictions on nearby cargo
choice_b: Upside down to prevent terminal corrosion
choice_c: Right side up so their liquid won't spill, with other cargo kept from falling against or short-circuiting them, and never with Division 1.1 explosives
choice_d: On their side to save space, and they may be loaded with any explosives
explanation: The manual requires charged storage batteries to be loaded right side up so liquid won't spill and protected from short-circuiting, and the Do Not Load Table specifies they must never be loaded with Division 1.1 explosives.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 8 (Corrosive) Materials / Do Not Load Table

topic: Class 2 Compressed Gas Cylinders - Securing
question: If your vehicle does not have racks to hold gas cylinders, how must the cylinders be secured during loading?
choice_a: Laid on their side with no restriction on valve position
choice_b: Stacked loosely as long as they do not touch the cab
choice_c: Held upright, or in racks/boxes that keep them from turning over, with horizontal loading allowed only if the relief valve is in the vapor space
choice_d: Secured only with rope, regardless of orientation
explanation: The manual requires cylinders to be held upright or placed in racks or boxes that prevent turning over, and allows horizontal loading only if designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 2 (Compressed Gases) Including Cryogenic Liquids

topic: Poison Materials Prohibited in the Driver's Cab
question: Where are you never allowed to load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD?
choice_a: Anywhere except the very rear of the trailer
choice_b: In the nose box of the trailer, as long as it is sealed
choice_c: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
choice_d: Next to other Division 6.1 poison packages only
explanation: The manual specifically prohibits loading a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Division 2.3 or Division 6.1 (Poisonous) Materials

topic: Class 7 Radioactive Materials - Total Transport Index Limit
question: What is the maximum total transport index allowed for all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages loaded together in a single vehicle?
choice_a: There is no numeric limit as long as packages are separated by two feet
explanation: The manual states that the total transport index of all radioactive packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Class 7 (Radioactive) Materials

topic: Segregation - Poison Materials and Foodstuffs
question: The Do Not Load Table generally prohibits loading Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison-labeled materials in the same vehicle as animal or human food. Which items are NOT considered foodstuff under this rule?
choice_a: Bagged grain and animal feed
choice_b: Canned vegetables and bottled water
choice_c: Mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams
choice_d: Fresh produce of any kind
explanation: The manual notes that foodstuffs are anything you swallow, but specifically excludes mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams from that definition.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.3 - Do Not Load Table

topic: Bulk Packaging Identification Number Display
question: How must the identification number of hazardous materials in a portable tank or other bulk packaging be displayed?
choice_a: Only inside the cab on the dashboard
choice_b: In black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background if no placards are required
choice_c: In any color numbers at least 1 mm tall, placed anywhere on the vehicle
choice_d: Painted directly onto the tires
explanation: The manual requires black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background when no placards are required.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 - Markings

topic: Portable Tank Marking Requirements
question: In addition to the identification number, what must a portable tank display, and how tall must the shipping name lettering be on a tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons?
choice_a: The lessee or owner's name and the shipping name on two opposing sides, with letters at least two inches tall
choice_b: Only the driver's name, in letters at least six inches tall
choice_c: The manufacturer's warranty information, in any size lettering
choice_d: The shipping name only, with no minimum letter height specified
explanation: The manual requires portable tanks to show the lessee or owner's name and the shipping name of the contents on two opposing sides, with letters at least two inches tall on tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 - Markings

topic: Cargo Tank Loading Attendant Requirements
question: The person watching a cargo tank during loading or unloading must meet several requirements. Which of the following is one of them?
choice_a: Be within 25 feet of the tank, with a clear view of it, and be authorized and able to move the cargo tank
choice_b: Be inside the cab with the doors locked at all times
choice_c: Have no knowledge of the material being loaded, to avoid bias
choice_d: Be within 500 feet of the tank so they are not exposed to fumes
explanation: The manual requires the attendant to be alert, have a clear view of the cargo tank, be within 25 feet of it, know the hazards and emergency procedures, and be authorized and able to move the cargo tank.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 - Tank Loading

topic: Closing Manholes and Valves Before Moving a Tank
question: Before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, what must you do regardless of how small the amount in the tank is?
choice_a: Nothing extra is required if the tank is nearly empty
choice_b: Fill the tank completely so nothing can shift
choice_c: Close all manholes and valves to prevent leaks
choice_d: Open all valves to relieve pressure before driving
explanation: The manual requires manholes and valves to be closed before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount or how short the distance, since it is illegal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers unless it is empty per 49 CFR 173.29.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 - Tank Loading

topic: Flammable Liquid Loading - Grounding Requirement
question: When filling a cargo tank with a flammable liquid through an open filling hole, when must the tank be grounded?
choice_a: Grounding is optional if the engine is left running
choice_b: Only during unloading, never during loading
choice_c: Only after the filling hole is closed
choice_d: Before opening the filling hole, maintaining the ground until after closing the filling hole
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to ground the tank before opening the filling hole and to maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 - Flammable Liquids

topic: Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives
question: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities such as fueling, how close may you park a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives to a bridge, tunnel, building, or place where people gather?
choice_a: Never within 300 feet
choice_b: Never within 50 feet
choice_c: There is no minimum distance as long as the vehicle is placarded
choice_d: Never within 1,000 feet
explanation: The manual states that, except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities like fueling, you must not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or open fire when loaded with these explosives.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 - Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

topic: Safe Haven for Unattended Explosives-Laden Vehicles
question: What is a 'safe haven' in the context of parking a vehicle loaded with explosives?
choice_a: Any well-lit parking lot with security cameras
choice_b: An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, usually designated by local authorities
choice_c: The driver's own home driveway
choice_d: A designated lane on the interstate highway
explanation: The manual defines a safe haven as an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, with designation usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 - Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

topic: Parking a Placarded Vehicle Not Carrying Explosives
question: If you are transporting placarded hazardous materials other than Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, when may you park within five feet of the traveled part of the road?
choice_a: Only overnight, if the vehicle's lights are left on
choice_b: At any time, with no restrictions
choice_c: Never, under any circumstances
choice_d: Only briefly, if your work requires it, and someone must always watch the vehicle
explanation: The manual states you may park a placarded vehicle not laden with explosives within five feet of the traveled road only if your work requires it, only briefly, and someone must always watch the vehicle.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.2 - Parking a Placarded Vehicle Not Transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

topic: Attending a Parked Placarded Vehicle
question: A person attending a parked placarded vehicle must be within what distance of the vehicle, with it in clear view, if not actually in the vehicle?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_b: 10 feet
choice_c: There is no distance requirement as long as a phone is available
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: The manual requires the attendant to be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle with it in clear view.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.3 - Attending Parked Vehicles

topic: No Flares Near Hazardous Materials
question: If you break down and need to use stopped vehicle warning signals, what must you use instead of flares or fuses near a tank of Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials, or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Nothing is required if the vehicle is parked off the roadway
choice_b: Reflective triangles or red electric lights
choice_c: A lit fusee held by the driver
choice_d: Road flares placed at least 50 feet away
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to use reflective triangles or red electric lights and never use burning signals such as flares or fuses around these tanks or explosive loads.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.4 - No Flares!

topic: Written Route Plan for Transporting Explosives
question: If you are transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must you have and follow while en route?
choice_a: A written route plan, prepared in advance and kept with you while transporting the explosives
choice_b: Only a GPS unit set to the fastest route
choice_c: A verbal route briefing from dispatch with no written record required
choice_d: No special route documentation is required for explosives
explanation: The manual requires drivers transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives to have a written route plan, prepared in advance by the carrier (or by the driver in certain cases), and to keep a copy of it while transporting the explosives.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 - Route Restrictions

topic: No Smoking Near a Placarded Vehicle While Driving
question: How close may you smoke to a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas)?
choice_a: You must not smoke within 25 feet of the tank
choice_b: You must not smoke within 5 feet of the tank
choice_c: There is no smoking restriction while driving, only while parked
choice_d: You may smoke as long as the windows are rolled up
explanation: The manual prohibits smoking within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases).
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.6 - No Smoking

topic: Refueling a Vehicle Carrying Hazardous Materials
question: What must you do before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials?
choice_a: Turn off your engine, and have someone always at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_b: Nothing special is required beyond normal fueling procedures
choice_c: Leave the engine running to maintain electrical power
choice_d: Disconnect the battery entirely before approaching the pump
explanation: The manual requires the engine to be turned off before fueling a vehicle containing hazardous materials, with someone always at the nozzle controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.7 - Refuel with Engine Off

topic: Fire Extinguisher Rating for Placarded Vehicles
question: What minimum fire extinguisher rating must the power unit of a placarded vehicle have?
choice_a: No specific rating is required, only that one be present
choice_b: A UL rating of 10 B:C or more
choice_c: A UL rating of 2 A:10 B:C or less
choice_d: A UL rating of 5 A only
explanation: The manual states that the power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.8 - 10 B:C Fire Extinguisher

topic: Checking Tires on a Placarded Vehicle
question: When must you examine each tire on a placarded motor vehicle, and how should you check tire pressure?
choice_a: Only at the start of the workday, using sound alone to judge pressure
choice_b: At the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked, using a tire pressure gauge
choice_c: Only once a week, by kicking each tire
choice_d: Only when a tire looks visibly low, by pressing it with your hand
explanation: The manual requires examining each tire at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked, and states that a tire pressure gauge is the only acceptable way to check tire pressure.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.9 - Check Tires

topic: Location of Shipping Papers While Driving
question: While you are behind the wheel of a vehicle carrying hazardous materials, where must the shipping papers be kept?
choice_a: Locked in the glove compartment out of sight
choice_b: Anywhere in the trailer, as long as they are with the cargo
choice_c: Within your reach with your seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door, easily seen by someone entering the cab
choice_d: In the sleeper berth, away from the driver's seat
explanation: The manual requires shipping papers to be kept within the driver's reach with the seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door, where they can be easily seen by someone entering the cab.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 - Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

topic: Equipment Required for Transporting Chlorine
question: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must carry which specific items in the vehicle?
choice_a: A second fire extinguisher rated 5 B:C
choice_b: A hazmat suit and a portable shower
choice_c: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
choice_d: Extra chlorine neutralizing tablets and a spare tank valve
explanation: The manual specifically requires a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks to have an approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.11 - Equipment for Chlorine

topic: Stopping at Railroad Crossings with Hazardous Materials
question: If your vehicle is placarded or carries any amount of chlorine, how far before the nearest rail must you stop at a railroad crossing?
choice_a: 100 to 200 feet before the nearest rail
choice_b: Between 15 and 50 feet before the nearest rail
choice_c: Exactly 5 feet before the nearest rail
choice_d: There is no specific distance, only that you stop somewhere before the tracks
explanation: The manual requires drivers of placarded vehicles or vehicles carrying any amount of chlorine to stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.6.12 - Stop before Railroad Crossings

topic: Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) Purpose
question: What is the purpose of the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG), and how is it indexed?
choice_a: It is a driver's log book required for hazmat endorsement renewal
choice_b: It is indexed alphabetically by carrier company name
choice_c: It helps firefighters, police, and industry workers protect themselves and the public from hazardous materials, and is indexed by proper shipping name and identification number
choice_d: It lists routes approved for hazardous materials transport in every state
explanation: The manual describes the ERG as a Department of Transportation guidebook for emergency personnel, indexed by proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.1 - Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)

topic: Driver's Duties at a Hazmat Crash Scene
question: As a commercial driver, what is your job at the scene of a hazardous materials crash or incident?
choice_a: Wait inside the cab with the doors locked until police arrive
choice_b: Keep people away from the scene, limit the spread of material only if you can safely do so, and communicate the danger to emergency responders
choice_c: Leave the scene immediately to avoid liability
choice_d: Personally contain and clean up any spilled material before help arrives
explanation: The manual lists the driver's duties as keeping people away from the scene, limiting the spread of material only if it can be done safely, and communicating the danger to emergency response personnel.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.2 - Crashes/Incidents

topic: Never Identify a Hazmat Leak by Smell
question: If you discover a cargo leak, why should you never try to identify the material or find the source of the leak by smell?
choice_a: Toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell
choice_b: It is only a concern for Class 8 corrosive materials
choice_c: Smelling the leak will always trigger a false positive on gas detectors
choice_d: Smell has no bearing on hazardous materials identification methods
explanation: The manual warns that toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell, so you should never try to identify a leak by smell.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.2 - Crashes/Incidents

topic: Feeling Trailer Doors Before Opening During a Fire
question: If you discover a fire and suspect a cargo fire in your trailer, why should you feel the trailer doors before opening them?
choice_a: If the doors are hot, opening them lets air in and may make the fire flare up, so you should not open them
choice_b: Feeling the doors tells you which hazard class is on fire
choice_c: Hot doors indicate the fire has already gone out
choice_d: It has no safety purpose; it is just a habit recommended for cold weather
explanation: The manual explains that if the doors are hot, opening them lets air in and may make the fire flare up, whereas without air many fires only smolder until firefighters arrive, doing less damage.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 - Fires

topic: Emergency Response for Class 7 Radioactive Spills
question: If radioactive material is involved in a leak or a broken package, what should you do?
choice_a: Wash the area with plain water immediately and resume driving
choice_b: Tell your dispatcher or supervisor as soon as possible, avoid touching or inhaling the material, and do not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter
choice_c: Sweep the material into a bag yourself and continue the trip
choice_d: Only report it if the transport index was greater than 10
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to tell their dispatcher or supervisor as soon as possible, avoid touching or inhaling the material, and not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 - Responses to Specific Hazards, Class 7 (Radioactive Materials)

topic: Notification Thresholds for the National Response Center
question: Which of the following requires you or your employer to notify the National Response Center after a hazardous materials incident?
choice_a: Any delay of more than 15 minutes in delivery
choice_b: Property damage of any amount over $500
choice_c: A single minor scrape to the trailer with no cargo involvement
choice_d: Estimated property damage exceeding $50,000, or a person killed
explanation: The manual lists a person being killed and estimated property damage exceeding $50,000 among the conditions requiring notification of the National Response Center.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 - Required Notification

topic: National Response Center vs. CHEMTREC
question: How do the National Response Center and CHEMTREC differ in their roles during a hazardous materials emergency?
choice_a: CHEMTREC is a government agency that issues fines, while the National Response Center is a private company
choice_b: They are the same organization operating under two different phone numbers for redundancy only
choice_c: The National Response Center coordinates emergency response as a resource for police and firefighters, while CHEMTREC provides technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials
choice_d: The National Response Center only handles radioactive materials, while CHEMTREC handles everything else
explanation: The manual describes the National Response Center as helping coordinate emergency response as a resource to police and firefighters, and CHEMTREC as providing emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 - Required Notification

topic: Hazardous Materials (H) Endorsement Requirement
question: Which driver must add a Hazardous Materials (H) endorsement to their CDL?
choice_a: Only drivers who work for a federal agency
choice_b: Only drivers of Class A combination vehicles
choice_c: Any driver, regardless of vehicle class, who wishes to haul a material required to be placarded, or any quantity of a material listed as a select agent or toxin
choice_d: Only drivers who transport materials in quantities under one pound
explanation: The manual states that any driver, regardless of vehicle Class/Group, who wishes to haul a material required to be placarded, or any quantity of a material listed as a select agent or toxin, must add a hazardous materials endorsement and pass a special written examination.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials (endorsement requirements as described in Section 1, CDL Endorsements)

topic: TSA Background Check for the Hazmat Endorsement
question: In order to obtain a hazardous materials endorsement, what must a driver undergo in addition to the special written examination?
choice_a: A Transportation Security Administration (TSA) background check reviewing criminal, immigration, and FBI records
choice_b: A physical fitness test administered by the state police
choice_c: A credit check performed by the carrier only
choice_d: A separate road test limited to tank vehicles
explanation: The manual states that the TSA and the US Department of Transportation require background checks, including a review of criminal, immigration, and FBI records, for commercial drivers certified to transport hazardous materials.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials (TSA background check requirements, described in Section 1.3.6, Hazardous Materials Endorsement Background Check and Disqualifications)

topic: Disqualifying Conditions for a Hazmat Endorsement
question: Which of the following will cause you to be denied, or to lose, a hazardous materials endorsement?
choice_a: Living more than 100 miles from your employer's terminal
choice_b: Having more than five years of driving experience
choice_c: Holding a Class B license instead of a Class A license
choice_d: Being considered a security threat as determined by the Transportation Security Administration, or not being a lawful permanent resident of the United States
explanation: The manual lists being considered a security threat as determined by the TSA, and not being a lawful permanent resident of the United States, among the conditions that will cause denial or loss of a hazardous materials endorsement.
source_note: Mississippi Commercial Driver's License Manual (AAMVA 'Modernized Testing System' base content, Version: July 2017), Mississippi Department of Public Safety (DPS) Driver Service Bureau -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials (endorsement disqualifications, described in Section 1.3.6, Hazardous Materials Endorsement Background Check and Disqualifications)
